newsitem.title: USA: Groups urge approval of Labor secretary nominee.
newsitem.headline: Groups urge approval of Labor secretary nominee.

text.p: Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle warned Thursday Democrats might use delaying tactics on Republican legislation if Republicans continued to block Alexis Herman's nomination as secretary of Labour.

The Senate Labour Committee approved Herman April 10 but Republican leaders have not allowed a final vote by the full Senate to protest President Clinton's pledge to issue an executive order that would force many companies with federal contracts to use union labour.

"My hope is that it (the Herman nomination) can come up next week. We're not in a very good position to allow any legislation to move forward until we've been able to resolve this in a meaningful way. So I'm hopeful that it can be done sooner rather than later," Daschle, of South Dakota, told reporters.
Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, said talks were under way with the administration to resolve the impasse. But he would not predict when a vote on Herman would take place.
Under Senate rules, any senator can block action on legislation unless at least 60 others vote to limit debate. Republicans have a 55-45 majority over Democrats.
Separately, a coalition of black, labour and women's groups Thursday attacked Lott and other Republicans for holding up Herman's confirmation.

"Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott's decision to hold hostage the floor vote on the nomination of Alexis Herman as secretary of Labour ... is absurd," Andrew Stern, president of the AFL-CIO's Service Employees International Union, said at a news conference.

"I urge Senator Lott and colleagues to schedule a U.S. Senate vote to confirm Alexis Herman -- an effective, qualified, competent leader -- to head the Department of Labour," Stern said. He was joined by representatives of the National Council of Negro Women, the Leadership Council on Civil Rights and the Women's Legal Defence Fund.
Clinton, who nominated Herman last December, criticised the delay Sunday in a speech to the United Auto Workers.
Herman, who was director of the White House Office of Public Liaison, would replace Robert Reich, who resigned at the end of Clinton's first term.
QUESTION: Does that mean no legislation will move forward until you resolve this?
